The model used for the glycol prototype was similar to the one used for Task 3 (Figure 13), but with only one fluid channel. The prototype was characterized using the experimental setup from Task 4 (Figure 17), but again with only one channel. The experimental results are shown in Figure 25, showing good agreement between model and experiment and that we can achieve ~3- minute discharge and maintain temperature below 15 °C. Figure 25: Discharge performance of high-power glycol prototype, with discharge periods of 1/10th hour, 1/15th hour, and 1/20th hour. Fluid outlet temperature rises to maintain constant power, and we generally see good agreement between the model and the experiment. For the second prototype, the model from Task 3 was modified to use a single channel with two- phase ammonia as the heat transfer fluid. The modeling results show a discharge period of ~3 minutes, with the temperature maintained below 16 °C (Figure 26). However, the discharge power does drop after 2.5 minutes, as shown in Figure 27. 28 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications.
